images.text:
My grandfather loved to tell us chilling stories. This was always one of my favourites – the story about the silent woman.
After the Depression had started in the 1930s, a lot of people were out of work. A woman came into a grocery store. She looked tired and hungry and pale. She was carrying two milk bottles. Wordlessly, she placed put them on the counter and the grocer picked them up. He exchanged them for full ones, saying: "Ten cents, please." She said nothing. She just took the bottles and left. He would have gone after her to demand his money if she hadn't looked so sad. He could see how hungry she was. He had always felt guilty because he had a job and food when others didn't. If he had not been so lucky, he would not be employed now. She had probably just lost her job, he decided. If she had had the money, she would have paid.

She came back again the next day as well with her empty bottles. He passed her two full ones and she hurried away. If she hadn't left so quickly, he would have spoken to her. The next morning she was there again. She looked so pale and tired that he felt badly for her. He wanted to talk to her. He wanted to offer her a job. However, before he was able to talk to her, she had run out of the store. After she had walked a block down the street, he followed her.

He was surprised to see her headed away from the town, down by the river and then into the graveyard there. He saw her hurry up to a headstone, where she seemed to disappear down into into the earth. He stood there shocked. He couldn't believe what he had seen.
Then, he heard something. It was the muffled cry of a baby. He moved toward the gravestone where he had last seen the woman and looked down. The sound was coming from beneath his feet!
He ran yelling down the street, calling for the police, for anyone to come. Within minutes, there was a swarm of people around the gravesite. When they heard the baby cry, they ran for shovels and started to dig.
When the casket was raised up out of the ground, a still hush came over the people standing around it as it was opened. The grocer looked in. The pale frail woman who had visited his store was laying dead inside it. In her arms, there was baby, and two full milk bottles. The baby squirmed and opened its eyes. It was still alive.

The Past Perfect Tense: Unreal Past
When you talk about the unreal past, you use past tenses to talk about hypothetical situations. You use the Past Perfect tense for unlikely or unreal situations in the past.
The structure of the Past Perfect tense is:
You use it with an If clause to contain the meaning of unreal past.
If I had known, I would have ...
This means you didn't know, but if you did you would have done something different.
Look at the following examples from the text:
If he had not been so lucky, he would not be employed now.
If she had had the money, she would have paid.
He would have gone after her to demand his money if she hadn't looked so sad.
If she hadn't left so quickly, he would have spoken to her.
The Present Perfect Tense and the Past Perfect Tense
You use the perfect tenses when you want to talk about events that are connected to another event in some way.
You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action that happened at an unspecified time in the past. You do not refer to any point in the time when you use the Present Perfect.
You also use the Present Perfect tense to talk about an action that started in the past and continues up to the present.
You use the Past Perfect tense to refer to a completed action in the past that happened before another past action.

I had studied German before I went to Germany.
First: I studied German,
Second: I went to Germany.
